name: The name as a monument
idea: The name is the headline. Set it so large that it becomes architecture: as wide as the margins allow, or stacked to fill the screen, every letter whole. Nothing else on the first screen competes; the description of what this is drops to a single small sentence. The idea comes from treating the name's letters as material. Ask what the subject can do to its own name: a photograph of the work stands behind it or opens under it, the name repeats down the page like a reel, the letters are split to opposite corners and the page happens between them (never a picture inside the letters or between the words). In the study this was the single most common device among sites scoring 7.5 or more.
composition: First screen: the wordmark spans the width between the page margins (font-size 16–24vw, set with a clamp so it never wraps), either whole on the bottom margin with no letter cut by any edge, or dead centre with everything else pushed to the corners. One line of supporting text at 16–20px sits in a corner on a shared margin; navigation is three or four words in the opposite corner. After the hero the page is deliberately small and calm: a narrow text column or a simple two-column grid, so the contrast with the monument holds. The footer is the dealt one, at text sizes: the name does not return there at full width. The name keeps the margins section 0 deals like everything else, every letter whole. Two type sizes do nearly all the work: the monument and a small text size, with one mid size for section headings.
typography: One family. The display cut must survive enormous sizes: tight tracking (-0.04 to -0.07em), leading 0.8–0.9, optical kerning on. Section headings are modest (28–40px) on purpose.
colour: Two values carry the page (ground and ink). The accent, if used at all, appears on one thing only: the single action.
imagery: Few images, set against the typography rather than as illustrations beside it: one photograph behind the name or directly above or under it, never inside it (no frame replacing a letter, nothing between its words), then a short run of large full-width or half-width photographs further down. Square corners. No collage of small thumbnails.
richness: Scale. The size of the name against the smallness of everything else is the entire visual event, so protect both ends: do not shrink the name to make room, and do not let body text creep above 20px.
pitfalls: A long name set small is just a logo. If the name has more than about 12 characters, stack it on two lines, every letter whole; never drop below 12vw. Do not add a second big headline under the name. Do not decorate the letters.

name: The sentence is the layout
idea: The page is an argument in plain sentences, each with its evidence beside it. The first screen is one short sentence about the subject that a visitor can check against the picture next to it ('Every loaf leaves the oven by six', beside the racks at six): the sentence sets the grid and the measure, and the picture stands beside it or opens full width right after it, never inside it. Write the sentences first, from the inventory, one claim each; then give each the one thing that proves it: a photograph, a figure, a short list, the product doing it. The reader believes the page because every sentence is shown.
composition: First screen: the sentence, four to seven words on two lines at the dealt display step, flush to the left margin across columns 1–7, with one supporting sentence and the action under it on the same edge. The picture it names fills columns 8–12 at the full height of the screen and ends on the right margin; or, when the sentence takes the full width, the picture runs across the width directly under it, cropped by the bottom of the screen (never on a software page: its interface stands beside the sentence). Later sections repeat the grammar at a smaller scale: a heading of one short sentence on the left half and its proof on the right half (a photograph, a figure with its unit, a short list, an interface fragment), top-aligned with it, so the page reads as a series of sentences with evidence. Every sentence starts on the same left edge, and no picture sits between words or between lines. The space between sections as section 0 deals it.
typography: Display weight with real presence (medium to bold), tracking -0.03 to -0.05em, leading 0.95–1.0 so two lines sit close. The sentences are real sentences: sentence case, with a full stop on every one or on none.
colour: A calm ground with ink at full contrast. The colour comes from the pictures beside the sentences; if the palette has an accent, use it once, on the action.
imagery: One strong photograph of what the first sentence says, large enough to check it against the words: beside the sentence on the first screen, or full width right after it. Every later picture is the proof of the sentence next to it, at a size that shows what it is. Never a picture inside a sentence, between its words or in its letters: that is a generated-page tell, and the inspector fails it.
richness: Sentences a reader can check, each paired with the thing that proves it. The first picture is read as the evidence for the headline, so choose it with care: it shows exactly what the sentence says, large.
pitfalls: The sentence must be short enough for two lines on a phone (about 32 characters). Do not style one word differently to stress it. Do not put a picture inside the sentence to make it an idea: the idea is the match between what the sentence says and what the picture shows. A sentence with no proof beside it is a slogan; cut it or find its proof.

name: The pinned poster
idea: Something stays put while everything else changes. A title holds its place across the viewport and the images beneath it swap; the name is split to two opposite corners and the page passes between the halves; a single frame stays centred while its contents change. Every scroll step is a new cover of the same magazine. The idea suits subjects that are a series (a book of portraits, a line-up, a collection, a set of projects): the fixed element says what the series is, the changing element shows its members.
composition: A sticky layer holds the fixed element for the height of two to three viewports: usually the title at 10–14vw across the middle or top of the screen, or two words pinned to the top-left and bottom-right corners. Under it, a stack of full-height panels scrolls by, each a single large photograph (portrait 4:5, centred, 40–50% of the viewport wide) with one line of caption at the same small size everywhere. The title sits above the images in the stacking order and uses `mix-blend-mode: difference` or a solid colour that reads on every panel. When the pinned run ends, the page releases into ordinary flowing sections with a narrow measure. Build with `position: sticky`; never hijack the scroll.
typography: The pinned title is the only large type on the page. Captions and body share one small size (15–17px). Tight tracking and solid weight so the title reads over photographs.
colour: One strong title colour against a pale or dark ground. Every panel stands on that ground or the surface tone; the photographs carry the other colours.
imagery: A series of photographs with the same crop ratio and the same framing (all portraits, all objects, all rooms), so that swapping them reads as one image changing. Five to eight in the pinned run.
richness: Repetition with change. The fixed title makes each new photograph feel like an event, so the photographs must be good and consistent.
pitfalls: If the title is not legible over every panel, the idea fails: test each one. Keep the pinned run under six viewports or it feels like a trap. On a phone the title shrinks to 16–18vw and stays pinned at the top; panels become full-width. A pin longer than three screens, or one where the screens under it are nearly empty, read in blind tests as a stuck page. Every screen under the pin needs its own content, and nothing may pass over the pinned words.

name: Colour chapters
idea: Every section is a chapter with its own flat colour, floor to ceiling. The page reads like a set of posters hung in a row, held together by one typeface and one grid. The colours are not decoration: they come from the subject (the brand's packaging, the artist's record sleeves, the product's own colour ways, the categories of the content) and each chapter's colour means that chapter. Decide the sequence like a designer orders a book: a strong opener, a quiet second, a surprise in the middle, a dark or very light closer.
composition: Sections are full-bleed fields, each at least 90svh tall, butted directly against each other with no gap and no divider. Inside every field the same 12-column grid and the same margins apply, and each field holds one thing: a huge heading (8–12vw) with a small paragraph, or one photograph with a caption, or one list. Text colour is chosen per field for strong contrast (ink or paper, never grey). Headings start on the same left edge in every chapter, so the eye feels the system as colours change. The navigation and the footer take the colours of the first and last chapter.
typography: One typeface in two weights. Headings very large and tight; body 18–20px. Because colour is loud, the type stays plain: no italics, no second face.
colour: Four to six flat fields used at full strength, one per section, each with its assigned text colour. No tints, no gradients between them: the hard edge where two fields meet is the look.
imagery: Sparing. One photograph or object per chapter at most, either cut out and sitting directly on the colour, or a plain rectangle with generous colour around it. Photographs should be simple enough not to fight the field.
richness: Colour at scale. A whole screen of one saturated colour is rich on its own, so a chapter needs few elements; it still needs its content at full size, because a coloured screen with one small line on it reads as empty.
pitfalls: Check contrast on every field with the palette's assigned ink. Do not put cards on the fields. Do not use more than six colours. Two neighbouring fields should differ clearly in lightness as well as hue.

name: The place carries it
idea: For a place, the photograph is the argument. One full-bleed image of where you would be standing fills the first screen, and the design steps back: the name sits whole on the bottom margin like a film title, or small in a corner, and nothing else interrupts the view. The page that follows keeps that restraint: few words, large pictures, long pauses. The designer's work here is editing: choosing the one frame that makes someone want to be there, and then not covering it.
composition: First screen: a single photograph at 100vw by 100svh, focal point kept clear of text. The name is set either very large (14–20vw) whole on the bottom margin, no letter cut by any edge, or small (20–28px) top-left with a one-line description bottom-left. Navigation is two to four words in the top corners in the same small size. If text sits on the image, a flat dark scrim under the text area only. Below, sections alternate between a short centred or left-set paragraph in a narrow column (max 52ch) with wide empty margins, and photographs shown large: one full-bleed, then a pair at different sizes, then one portrait offset to the right. Practical information (hours, address, rates, booking) is gathered once near the end in a plain two-column block.
typography: A face with some grace for the name; small, calm, well-spaced text everywhere else. Sentence case. Body 17–19px with leading around 1.55.
colour: Neutral paper or deep neutral ground chosen to flatter the photographs; text ink drawn from the darkest tone in the imagery. Colour lives in the pictures.
imagery: The dealt set is the palette. Choose four to six photographs with the same light. The hero image must have a calm area for the name. Full-bleed or large with square corners; never thumbnails, never a carousel of ten.
photoTreatment: Leave photographs ungraded. If text overlays one, darken only the area behind the text with a flat dark scrim.
richness: The photographs, at full size, uninterrupted. Empty paper around short text makes the next image land harder.
pitfalls: A weak hero photograph cannot be fixed by typography; pick again. Do not stack a headline, a paragraph and two buttons on the image. Do not use a booking bar that covers the bottom of the view; one small action is enough.

name: The page is the object
idea: Find the printed or physical artefact that already exists in the subject's world and build the page as that thing. A wedding site is the invitation card. A restaurant is its menu. A conference is the ticket; a record is its sleeve; a shop is the receipt or the swing tag; an archive is its catalogue card; a course is the syllabus sheet. The artefact supplies everything a template would otherwise invent: its proportions, its typographic manners, its way of grouping information. Visitors recognise the object instantly, which is why these pages feel specific.
composition: The first screen sets the artefact's proportions and manners on the page's own ground, not a panel on a field: a menu's tall column and tidy price alignment, a ticket's wide format with its facts in aligned cells, an invitation's centred symmetry. All primary content is set the way that object is set; the ground is a flat colour, with one photograph beside the words where the subject has one. As the page continues, each group that belongs together (the courses, the ticket's details, the dates) stands in the card style section 0 deals, with straight edges: never scallops, notches, perforations or an outlined box.
typography: Take the manners of the artefact: a bookish serif with small caps avoided, or a blunt condensed face for tickets and posters. Sizes stay within what print would use relative to the panel; the name is large on the panel, details are small and exact.
colour: Paper and ink plus the ground the paper sits on. Two or three flat colours in total, like a two-colour print job.
imagery: Optional. One photograph beside the words, or small photographs set like tipped-in plates. The artefact's manners are the image.
richness: Recognition. The print-like proportions and alignment and the limited inks make a familiar object out of plain HTML.
pitfalls: Choose an artefact that truly belongs to the subject, or it becomes costume. The object shows in its proportions, its type manners and its grouping, never in drawn edges: no notches, scallops, perforations or dotted borders, and no outlined rectangle. Keep text sizes readable on a phone.

name: One motif
idea: Take one shape from the subject and let it run the whole system. A drilling tool's octagonal cross-section becomes the buttons, the image masks and the loader. A two-account money app becomes two circles that recur as icon, inline dot and section colour. A café's striped awning becomes every band on the page. Look at the product, the logo, the object or the word in the headline and find the simplest geometry in it (a circle, an arc, a chamfer, a stripe, a notch, a ring). Then use only that shape, at three or four very different scales, everywhere a designer would normally reach for a generic rounded rectangle.
composition: Hero: the motif appears once at enormous scale as a flat filled shape, cropped by the viewport (a circle 120vh across entering from the right, a chamfered block filling the lower half), with a short headline at 6–8vw and one supporting sentence set on the remaining ground, left-aligned on a shared margin. Through the page the motif returns as: the mask for every photograph (via `clip-path` or `border-radius` made from the same geometry), the shape of the primary button, the bullet beside list items at text size, and one full-width band that separates the two halves of the page. Sections use simple two-column or single-column layouts so the shape is the only thing with character.
typography: A clean geometric or grotesk face that echoes the shape (round bowls for circles, squared terminals for chamfers). Medium weight; headings 6–8vw in the hero and 3–4vw after.
colour: The motif carries the accent colour at large scale, flat. Everything else is ground and ink. A second motif colour is allowed only if the subject has a real pair (two accounts, two modes).
imagery: Photographs appear inside the motif's shape. If there is product interface to show, it sits on a flat colour stage shaped by the motif. Draw the shape with CSS or a simple inline SVG path; do not draw illustrations.
richness: One shape at many sizes. The giant cropped shape gives the hero mass and colour without a single image.
pitfalls: One motif means one. A circle here, a hexagon there and a blob behind is the generated look this replaces. The motif must come from the subject and you must be able to say from where in one clause.

name: The product performs
idea: Software is most convincing when it is doing its job in front of you. Instead of describing features, put small, true, working fragments of the product on the page: the actual control, with real content, responding to the pointer. A colour picker's loupe reads the page's own background and prints its value. A list tool lets you tick an item right there. A type-scale plugin sets the page's own headings. Find the one interaction that is the product and make the hero that interaction; then show each further capability as another fragment at real size. No dashboard collage, no browser frame, no screenshots shrunk until unreadable.
composition: Hero: a short plain headline (5–6vw, left-aligned, upper-left third) and one sentence; the rest of the first screen is the main fragment at actual interface size, sitting directly on the page or on one flat stage colour, large enough to read every label. The fragment is built in HTML and works. Below, capabilities are a single-column sequence, each a row of two parts on a 5/7 split: a two-line statement on one side and the relevant fragment on the other, with the fragments varying in size and shape so the column never becomes a zigzag of equal blocks. Fragments are cropped pieces of interface (a menu, a row, a control, a panel edge), not whole windows. One section pins a fragment while three short statements change it.
typography: The marketing type matches the product's interface type so the fragments and the page feel like one thing. Headline plain in its words, never small: beside the main fragment it is 5vw or more at 1440 (72px); interface text at its true size (13–15px) inside fragments.
colour: Neutral ground. The product's own interface colours provide the colour. At most one flat stage colour behind fragments.
imagery: The interface fragments are the main imagery: build them carefully with real labels, real numbers and sensible states (one hovered, one selected). Around them, two or three real pictures of the customer's world (found with scripts/assets.mjs), never stock of people at laptops.
richness: Fidelity. A fragment with believable content and a real hover state is more interesting than any illustration. Spend the effort there.
pitfalls: A fake interface made of grey bars and circles is the worst outcome; if you cannot build a believable fragment, change direction. Mark each fragment's root element with the attribute data-ui: inside it the product's own conventions apply (1px control borders, small radii, a shadow on its open menu) and the inspector leaves them alone; outside it the house rules hold as usual. data-ui is for cropped fragments only, never for a page wrapper. Do not put the fragment in a browser or laptop frame.

name: The quiet instrument
idea: Radical understatement. Where every competitor shouts, this page almost whispers: a headline barely larger than body text, a narrow column, small exact demonstrations, and a great deal of untouched space. The restraint is the claim. It says the thing is simple, finished and sure of itself. This only works when it is carried through completely; one loud element breaks it. In the study, a tool for simple lists sold itself with a 27px headline and 12–14px copy and was one of the most confident pages in the set.
composition: A single column 440–560px wide, placed left of centre (starting at about 22% of the viewport width) or dead centre, running the whole page. The headline is the one large thing on the first screen: two lines at display size (5–7vw), medium weight, starting on the column's left edge and allowed to run wider than the column. The supporting paragraph follows at body size (17–19px) in the full ink. One small primary button and one text link. Below, each point is a short paragraph followed by a compact demonstration or image no wider than the column. Sections are separated only by space (the gap section 0 deals). Nothing spans the full width until the footer, the one full-width section, built as section 0 deals it. The first screen is mostly empty and that emptiness is composed: the column's top edge sits at about 30% of the viewport height.
typography: One family, two weights. A display size for the headline (5–7vw), one heading size for section titles (about 32–40px), body at 17–19px, a small size for captions (14–15px). Leading 1.5 for text. Letter-spacing near zero. The typeface must be handsome at small sizes.
colour: Paper and two inks (full and soft). One accent used on exactly one element per screen.
imagery: Precise rather than loud: cropped interface details at true size, and real photographs of the customer's world held to the column width, each doing one job. One short looping clip can sit at column width too. Never a large stock hero image.
richness: Precision. With so little on the page, alignment, spacing and the exact size relationships are the design. Every element shares the column's left edge.
pitfalls: This is the one direction where a small headline is right; the inspector will not object, but do not mix it with a large display line. Emptiness must look decided: keep the column edges exact and the vertical rhythm even. Not suitable when the subject needs emotion or photography to sell. Quiet is not thin: the column must still deliver every piece of content the brief asks for, in full, at 16px or more in the full ink. In blind tests the quiet version lost every time it was quiet everywhere: a small headline beside an empty panel read as unfinished. Quiet means few things, not small things: the headline and the demonstration are large, and every screen holds content.

name: The object, large
idea: Show the thing, bigger than seems reasonable. One photographed object fills the first screen, scaled until the viewport crops it, with the text small and tucked beside or behind it. The crop is the idea: a record whose edge leaves the top-right corner, a bottle whose shoulder runs off the bottom, a chair seen so close you read its grain. Being that close reads as confidence in the object. Everything else on the page serves it: details as tight close-ups, facts as short lines, one way to buy.
composition: First screen: the object occupies 55–75% of the viewport and breaks at least one edge. It sits on a flat field (ground colour or one bold colour), never in a box. The headline is short and either very large and partly hidden behind the object (10–13vw, the object overlapping two or three letters) or small (28–36px) in the opposite corner with a one-line description, and small only when the object stands in the middle of a wide field with the words well clear of it: beside an object that holds one half of a split, the headline is 5vw or more at 1440 (72px). No navigation bar beyond a wordmark and one action. Following sections: a row of three or four close-up details at different crop ratios (not equal tiles), a single wide photograph of the object in use, a plain list of facts set large (materials, size, price) aligned to one edge, then the purchase action. The object returns once at the end from a different angle.
typography: Either very large and structural or very small and precise; pick one for the headline and hold it. Facts are set in the text face at 22–28px, not in a table.
colour: A flat field chosen to make the object's own colour sing (its complement, or a tone darker than its shadow side). One field for the whole page, or a second for the facts section.
imagery: Use the product's own photographs if they exist. Otherwise the product is shown by its product statement (the sheet's hard rule), never another maker's, and the dealt set gives the still-lifes round it. Prefer images with a plain background; use `mix-blend-mode: multiply` on light fields so a white studio background disappears into the page colour.
photoTreatment: Scale the main image well past its container (`width: 120–160%`) and let `overflow: hidden` on the section do the cropping.
richness: The object's surface at close range, and the tension of the crop.
pitfalls: A small centred product shot with space all round is a catalogue thumbnail, not this direction. If the image has a busy background it cannot sit on a field; crop tighter or change image. Keep text off the object's focal area.

name: The specimen catalogue
idea: Present what is on offer the way a field guide presents birds: each item alone on the same plain field, same scale, same angle, named plainly. A bakery's pastries become specimens and the specimens become the menu. A furniture maker's chairs each stand alone in the same pale frame. The format flatters ordinary objects because it treats each as worth looking at, and it replaces both the feature grid and the product-card grid with something that has a point of view.
composition: Hero: a left-aligned statement of what this is (5–7vw, upper-left) beside or above a tight cluster of four to seven specimen tiles of different sizes arranged as a loose mosaic that ends on the right margin. Each tile is a square or 4:5 rectangle in one fill, the page's surface one step off the ground, with one photograph centred on it, no border, 8–12px gaps. The main section is the catalogue itself: a grid of tiles in which each item has its name and one fact set beneath the tile in the text face, aligned left to the tile edge. Every tile takes that same fill: the items carry the colour, never the tiles. One tile in every six or seven is double size. Supporting sections (about, how to order) are plain text on the ground colour, kept short.
typography: Friendly and plain. Item names at 18–22px in medium weight, facts beneath in the soft ink. One big statement in the hero; no other display type.
colour: The items are the colour. The ground stays quiet and every tile takes one fill, the surface a step off the ground; the accent goes on the action only. Tiles in three or four colours read as a wall of boxes and spread the palette (the inspector fails it, tile-wall).
imagery: Photographs of single items on plain backgrounds, all cropped to sit at the same apparent size within their tile. On pale tiles, `mix-blend-mode: multiply` removes white studio backgrounds. If the subject's own item photographs are missing, use the dealt set and say so, never another maker's product as an item (the sheet's hard rule).
richness: Rhythm of like objects on one ground and the pleasure of comparing like with like.
pitfalls: It needs at least six items that can be shown as objects; with three it is a feature row. Keep labels outside the tiles. No shadows under the objects, no hover lift.

name: Dressed as something else
idea: Art-direct the subject as if it belonged to a different, more vivid category. A money app is sold like a streetwear drop. An industrial roaster is presented like a design object. Drilling hardware gets the calm of a watch brand. A parcel-locker service becomes a fairground of stickers. Choose the borrowed category by asking what feeling the audience is missing from this kind of product (swagger, calm, glamour, play) and which category owns that feeling. Then take its manners completely: its type, its pacing, its way of photographing things. The contrast between dull subject and vivid dress is what people remember.
composition: Depends on the borrowed category, so decide it explicitly and write it in your notes. Fashion drop: one shouted condensed headline across the full width, a single cropped image under it, then product facts as a blunt list. Watch or perfume: a centred object on a dark field, a small serif name, very few words, long vertical pauses. Poster or zine: flat colour blocks, heavy type, tilted cut-out images. Museum: one item per screen on a plinth-like band of colour with a short label beside it. Whichever you choose, the page structure stays simple (four to six sections) and every section uses the borrowed manners, including pricing and the footer.
typography: The borrowed category's type, fully committed: condensed and loud, or refined and small. No halfway.
colour: The borrowed category's palette, which will be unlike the subject's sector norm. That mismatch is intended.
imagery: Photograph the subject the way the borrowed category would be photographed. With the dealt set, choose images for attitude, not literal relevance, and crop them hard.
richness: Attitude. The page has a recognisable voice from another world, applied to a subject nobody expected it for.
pitfalls: Name the borrowed category in one word before you start, or the result is merely loud. The content must still be clear: what it is, what it costs, how to get it. Avoid borrowing from 'tech startup', which is the default you are escaping.

name: The contact sheet
idea: Show everything at once, small, in order. The work is laid out like a photographer's contact sheet or an archive drawer: dozens of small frames in strict rows, with all text set at one small size. Nothing is featured, which is the point: the volume and consistency of the body of work is the statement, and the visitor does the choosing. It suits people and studios whose strength is range and output.
composition: The name, or one sentence about the work, sits at display size (6–9vw) across the top of the first screen, and the sheet begins directly under it, still inside the first screen. The first screen opens with three or four short blocks of small text across the top on a 12-column grid (who, what, where to reach them), all at 14–16px, and immediately below, the sheet begins: rows of thumbnails at a fixed height (90–140px) with their natural widths, 6–10px gaps, each project forming a run of four to eight frames preceded by its title in the same small text. The sheet fills the whole page width edge to edge with 16–20px margins. Hovering a run dims the others and shows that project's one-line description in a fixed position. A single enlarged frame may interrupt the sheet once per screen at four times the size.
typography: One face. The name at display size on the first screen; everything else at one text size and one small size; hierarchy below the name comes from position and from a single brighter ink for titles.
colour: Black or white ground, so the thumbnails are the only colour.
imagery: Many images: at least 24 frames to make a sheet. They are the client's own work (stills, title cards, page captures), never stock photographs standing in for it; with fewer pieces, a smaller sheet of the pieces there are. Square corners, no captions on the frames.
richness: Density and order. The mass of small images forms a texture; the strict rows keep it calm.
pitfalls: With fewer than about 20 images it looks unfinished; choose another direction. Do not add a big headline above the sheet. On a phone the frames become two per row at a fixed height and each run scrolls sideways. Rows that run past the right edge read as clipped in screenshots and to most visitors: wrap the frames onto the next line, or end each row inside the grid.

name: The printed annual
idea: Lay the page out like a well-designed printed report or magazine feature: a masthead image, a tight oversized title, text held to a strict column line, and colour used in solid blocks the way a two-colour print job would. It gives weight and authority to subjects that are really about content: findings, a manifesto, a programme, a serious product. The reader should feel that someone edited this.
composition: A fixed vertical axis at about 42% of the viewport width organises everything: headings begin on it, body columns hang from it, and the 0–42% zone holds small side notes, figures or stays empty. Masthead: a wide image band (photographic mosaic or a single crop) across the top 45% of the first screen; below it the title at 7–9vw starting on the axis, with a two-sentence standfirst at 20–24px. Sections are mostly text pages (title on the axis, body in one or two columns of 34–40ch to its right); once or twice a full-bleed colour page, in a band section 4 deals, carries one large figure, quotation or image mosaic. Mosaics are gutterless: photographs and tiles of the surface tone or the accent butted together in a 4- or 6-cell grid. Page numbers, running heads and other print furniture are left out.
typography: A tight heavy grotesk or a sharp serif for titles; an excellent text face for reading at 18–20px with leading near 1.5. Headings in sentence case, tracked tight.
colour: Paper, ink and the accent, like a two-colour print job. A colour page is a whole section in the ink or the accent, as section 4 deals its bands; every other section stands on the paper.
imagery: Photographs used as blocks in mosaics alongside flat colour tiles; mixed subjects are fine if cropped tight and given one treatment, the one section 0 deals.
photoTreatment: Give all photographs in a mosaic the one treatment section 0 deals, never mixed: in full colour unless it deals black-and-white.
richness: The column line, the mosaics and whole pages of colour give structure and variety without ornaments.
pitfalls: The axis must be exact and reused everywhere or it reads as random indentation. Keep paragraphs to a real reading measure. On a phone the axis collapses to the left margin and side notes move inline above their paragraph.

name: Loud and flat
idea: A page with the directness of a street poster: flat saturated colour, the heaviest type you can find, short blunt statements, and photographs cut out and stuck on. It is for subjects with a voice. Write the page as things a person would actually say out loud, and let the design say them at full volume. The craft is in the control beneath the noise: a strict grid, two or three colours, and exact alignment keep it from becoming a mess.
composition: Hero: a statement of three to six words in ultra-heavy type at 11–15vw, filling the width, lines stacked tight (leading 0.85), flush left with 20–28px margins, on a flat saturated ground. One cut-out or hard-cropped photograph overlaps the type from the right or bottom, tilted 3–6 degrees. A single chunky button in the contrasting flat colour. Sections are solid panels on the page's grounds in turn (the ground, the surface tone, and once the band section 4 deals in the ink or the accent): one is a row of short statements each on its own panel of unequal width; one is a single photograph bleeding off two edges with a caption block set over a solid colour bar; one is a large plain list. Panels meet edge to edge. Corners are square or use one large radius (28–40px) consistently.
typography: The heaviest weight available, set tight, mostly lowercase or mostly uppercase (choose one). Body text is a plain grotesk at 18–20px.
colour: Flat colour at full strength from the dealt roles alone: the ground, the ink (black or white) and the accent, with the surface tone for panels. Each panel is one of them; text on it is one other.
imagery: Photographs with attitude, cropped hard or cut to a simple shape with `clip-path` (circle, arch, blunt polygon), slightly rotated, overlapping the type. Two or three on the page.
richness: Colour mass, type mass, and overlap.
pitfalls: Headlines still obey the two-line rule: at 13vw that means very few words, which is correct for this voice. No outlines, no offset shadows, no sticker confetti. Rotation is for two or three images only, never for text blocks.

name: The split stage
idea: For the first screens, half the screen does not move. One side is a fixed photograph (or object, or product view) that holds while the first sections pass; the other side is a calm scrolling column with what you read first. The fixed half keeps the feeling present while the reader gets the first facts, like sitting in the room while reading the menu. Then it lets go, and the rest of the page opens to the full width.
composition: Desktop: the first screen and one or two sections after it are a two-column stretch, 50/50 or 45/55. One column is `position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100svh` and holds a single photograph filling it edge to edge, or the object centred on a flat field. The other column scrolls in a single narrow measure (max 46ch) with comfortable padding (48–72px): name and one-line description first, then one or two sections separated by generous space. Headings in the scrolling column are modest (32–44px). The column grounds differ: photograph on one side, flat paper colour on the other, meeting at a clean vertical edge. Then the sticky half releases: the sections after it run on the full width in shapes of their own (a full-bleed photograph, a table across the width, a list on 8 of 12 columns), at least one of them full width, and never the picture-and-text split two sections running. On a phone the fixed half becomes a 60svh image at the top that stays sticky behind the first section, then releases.
typography: A text-first setting: a readable serif or a calm sans at 17–19px, with one display size for the name. Left-aligned throughout.
colour: The paper colour of the reading column is chosen against the photograph: a tone taken from its shadows or its lightest area. One ink, optionally one accent ink for links and the action.
imagery: One excellent portrait-orientation photograph for the fixed half, plus one or two more that crossfade in as their sections arrive, and large ones of its own for the full-width sections after it. Small photographs between the paragraphs of the reading column, never inside a sentence, are optional and should be few.
richness: A full-height photograph in view through the first screens, against a quiet, well-set column of text, then the page opening to the full width.
pitfalls: The reading column must be genuinely well typeset. Do not put cards or grids in it. Check that the fixed image crops well at short viewport heights. In blind tests the commonest complaint was monotony: several screens of the same split with only the text changing (a cargo-bike page ran 50/50 blocks all the way down). Release the sticky half after one or two sections, and never set two sections in a row as the same picture-and-text split.

name: The well-kept board
idea: The whole page is a board of tiles fitted edge to edge with narrow gaps, like a tidy desk seen from above. Each tile is one thing: the name, a statement, a photograph, a number, a link, a short list. There is no hero and no sequence of bands; the page is one continuous composition that the eye roams. It suits subjects with many small true things to show (a studio with work, writing, clients and news; a product with several distinct capabilities) and it replaces the generic bento by having real content in every tile and a strict system for sizes.
composition: A 12-column grid with 8px gaps and 8–12px outer margins, filled completely, no empty cells. Tiles use only four sizes (for example 6×4, 6×2, 3×2, 3×4 in column × row units of about 90px). Every tile is a flat filled rectangle: ground colour one step from the page, or a palette colour, or a photograph covering it. One radius everywhere (0, or 6–10px). The first screen contains: a name tile (the name at display size, the largest type on the page) with the wordmark set large, a statement tile with the description at 28–40px, two or three image tiles and one action tile in the accent colour. Text inside tiles is top-left aligned with 20–24px padding and never centred. Below the first screen the board continues with the same sizes; the last row is the footer made of tiles.
typography: One grotesk in two weights. Inside tiles: a large size for single statements, a small size for lists. No uppercase labels in tile corners.
colour: Page ground, tile ground one step lighter or darker, and one or two palette colours on selected tiles. Photographs supply the rest.
imagery: Photographs fill whole tiles with `object-fit: cover`; choose images that crop well to both wide and tall tiles.
richness: The fit. A full board with consistent gaps and varied tile contents is satisfying in the way a packed suitcase is.
pitfalls: Tiles are filled, never outlined, and never carry shadows. Do not put an icon and a two-line feature blurb in every tile; vary what tiles hold. Decide the phone layout as its own board: two columns, tiles re-ordered so the name and statement lead.

name: Photographs at uneven sizes
idea: A calm page where the pictures are placed like prints on a gallery wall: each at its own size and position, with text set small and light between them. Nothing lines up in the obvious way, yet everything sits on a grid you can feel. The unevenness is what makes it read as art-directed by a person: a small portrait far left, a wide landscape ending on the right margin, a square set lower than both. It lets photographs lead without ever becoming a slideshow.
composition: A 12-column grid with wide margins (5–7vw). The hero is a single line of large light type (6–9vw) across the top third, and below it one photograph placed off-centre (columns 6–12, 16:10), its top edge overlapping the baseline zone of the headline by a few pixels of deliberate tension. Each following section places two or three photographs with different spans and vertical offsets: for example a 3:4 portrait in columns 2–5 starting 120px lower than a 16:10 landscape in columns 7–12; then a single small 1:1 in columns 9–11 beside a paragraph in columns 2–6. Paragraphs are short (max 40ch) and sit in the gaps. No two consecutive sections use the same arrangement. Vertical spacing is large and irregular on purpose (120–260px).
typography: A light or regular weight at large size for the few headings; small, quiet text. Serif or a slender sans. Everything left-aligned to grid lines.
colour: A pale neutral ground with one deep ink taken from the photographs. No accent beyond a quiet link colour.
imagery: Six to nine photographs from one set, in a deliberate mix of ratios (3:4, 4:5, 1:1, 16:10, 21:9). Square corners. Captions, if any, are one short line under an image in the soft ink.
richness: Placement. The differing sizes and offsets create movement on a still page.
pitfalls: Uneven is not random: every image edge lands on a column line, and offsets come from a small set of values. On a phone, keep the unevenness with alternating widths (100%, 72% left, 60% right) rather than stacking everything full width.

name: The dark room
idea: One dark field from top to bottom, and in it, lit things. Photographs and objects appear like exhibits in a dim gallery: each with space around it, each the brightest thing on its screen. Type is light, small and sparse. The darkness is not a theme switch; it is a room, and the page is a slow walk through it. It suits subjects sold on atmosphere and material: an evening restaurant, a metal card, a record, a house at dusk.
composition: A single near-black or deep-toned ground runs the full page with no section bands. First screen: either the name at full width in a light weight whole on the bottom margin with one dim photograph above it, or one object or photograph centred at 40–50% of the viewport with a line of text beneath at 16–18px. Each later screen holds one or two lit items at a generous size (the main one 40–60% of the screen width) with its text set beside it at full reading size; the darkness frames the items, it does not replace content. Images vary in size but all share the same darkness at their edges so they sit in the ground without frames. Practical details come last in a simple two-column text block. The only solid light element on the page is the single primary action.
typography: Light or regular weights; they glow on dark. Avoid heavy bold, which looks cheap on black. Headings 4–7vw at most; text 16–18px with leading 1.6 and a slightly lifted ink (not pure white).
colour: A dark ground with a tint (blue-black, green-black, brown-black), a soft light ink, a dimmer ink for secondary text, and one warm or bright accent used once per screen at most.
imagery: Low-key photographs: dark backgrounds, one light source, subjects emerging from shadow. Their dark edges should blend into the page ground.
photoTreatment: If a photograph's background is lighter than the page, darken the image slightly (`filter: brightness(0.85) contrast(1.05)`) rather than adding a frame.
richness: Light against dark, and the slow pacing.
pitfalls: Grey text on black fails contrast quickly: check it. No glow effects, no neon accent, no coloured light blobs. A dark page with a bright busy photograph is not this direction; choose low-key images. Dark does not mean empty: every screen still carries its content at a readable size, and running text is a light ink at 7:1 or more, not a dim grey.

name: Type and nothing else
idea: The first screen is made only of words, colour and space, good enough that nobody misses a picture there. Pictures arrive later, large and few, as relief from the type. This is the honest answer when a subject has nothing worth photographing: instead of inventing illustrations, set what you have to say as well as it can be set. The typography carries a point of view through scale (one enormous statement, everything else small), through measure (a narrow, bookish column or a full-width line), and through one committed colour.
composition: First screen: the statement, two lines at most, set at 9–14vw and occupying the full width with tight leading, positioned in the upper two-thirds. One supporting sentence at 20–24px sits bottom-left on the same margin and the single action sits bottom-right on the same baseline. No navigation bar; two or three links in a top corner. Sections that follow are typographic set pieces, each different: a list of five to eight capabilities set at 4–6vw one per line; a paragraph at 28–36px in a 28ch column pushed to the right half; a pair of large numerals with a sentence each; a single quotation filling a colour field. Each section uses a different horizontal position (left, right, full) so the page has movement without imagery.
typography: This direction lives or dies on the face and its settings. Display at tight tracking and leading; text sizes few and far apart (for example 15, 22, 34 and the display size). Use real typographic detail: proper quotes, balanced line breaks, hung punctuation where it helps.
colour: Either one saturated ground for the whole page with a single ink, or paper and ink with one section inverted and one in the accent as a full field. Colour does the job images would have done.
imagery: The first screen has no picture. Further down, real pictures of the subject's world (found with scripts/assets.mjs) arrive large and few: a full-bleed photograph between two type sections, a looping clip in one band, a sharp modern photograph beside a list. Do not add icons, shapes, patterns or abstract graphics to compensate for anything.
richness: Scale contrast and colour mass. A capability list set at 5vw is an image in its own right.
pitfalls: Without pictures, weak copy has nowhere to hide: write real sentences. Vary the set pieces; four sections of big-heading-plus-paragraph is a text document, not a design. Keep all headings within two lines.

name: The product, clearly
idea: Explain the product the way the best technology companies do: one plain sentence that says what it is and who it is for, then the product itself, large and real, then each thing it does shown rather than told. The idea is not a metaphor; it is the product's own best moment, chosen and framed so a visitor understands it in five seconds. Find the one screen, object or result that makes someone want it, and open with that.
composition: The first screen is a confident headline (the dealt display step, which the sheet raises to 5vw at 1440 when the words sit beside the product; two lines at most), one sentence under it and one or two actions, with the product filling most of what is left: a large interface fragment, the object, or the result it produces (software sets its interface beside the headline, never under it). Below it the page alternates between wide product moments (one capability, one picture or fragment at full width with a short heading) and compact rows that pair two sentences with a cropped fragment. Somewhere in the middle a calm overview lists the remaining capabilities as short items (a name and one sentence each), set in two or three columns with no icons and no boxes. Facts that matter (prices, limits, platforms, numbers) are set as facts: a table, a list, a figure. Sections are separated by space, not by colour.
typography: Sentence case everywhere. The headline is large but not a poster (about 5vw at 1440 beside the product); the hierarchy comes from weight and space as much as from size. Interface text inside fragments at its true size.
colour: A neutral ground (white, off-white or near-black) for the whole page; the accent on the actions and links only. Any other colour comes from the product itself.
imagery: The product is the picture: real interface fragments (data-ui), the object photographed or generated as it is (without its own photographs, its product statement, never another maker's), or the output it makes. Few people photographs; none of people at laptops.
richness: Fidelity and order. A real fragment with believable content, a well-organised overview, numbers that add up and a footer that works carry more than any effect.
pitfalls: Boxes everywhere (every capability in its own card), icons above feature names, three identical columns, a hero headline of ten words, a giant gradient. If the product cannot be shown truthfully, show its output or its facts instead of a fake dashboard.

name: The shop window
idea: Build the page the way the best shops do: the products and the world they belong to, in large, sharp photographs, and an obvious way to buy. Taste shows in restraint: what is left out, how the pictures are cropped, how little the copy says. Find what makes this shop's things worth owning (a material, a maker, a place) and let every picture show it.
composition: The first screen is one large photograph (or two side by side) with a short line and the action; the navigation names the real categories. Then products in rows of two to four, each a picture, a name and a price, nothing more. Between product rows, one editorial band: a single large picture with two sentences about the material or the making. A short row of the facts buyers ask about (delivery, returns, care) in plain text. The footer is link columns with a sign-up.
typography: Small and calm. Product names and prices at the body size; headings modest; the pictures carry the scale.
colour: White or a pale neutral ground; ink near-black; one quiet accent or none (the action in the ink). Colour comes from the products.
imagery: The products, photographed (or generated) consistently: one background, one light, one crop per row. Around them, a few pictures of the world they are used in. No mock-ups, no floating cut-outs with shadows, no lifestyle stock of smiling models.
richness: The products themselves, many of them, sharp and well ordered; the editorial band; real prices and real facts.
pitfalls: Few, small or inconsistent product pictures; copy that explains instead of showing; badges and labels on every product; a carousel of three; a giant brand name at the foot.

name: The calm magazine
idea: Treat the page like a well-made magazine: a few things worth reading and looking at, given room. The subject's story is told in short pieces, each with one good picture and a few lines, in the order a reader would want them. The idea comes from what this subject has to say that nobody else can.
composition: A first screen that reads like a cover: one large picture and a title, or a title alone with generous space and one line under it. Then a sequence of short pieces, each with its own shape: a wide picture with a caption-free heading under it, a two-column spread (picture on one side, a short text on the other), a list of dated items, a single quotation set as text. Pictures change size from piece to piece so the rhythm never repeats. Text columns are narrow (about 60 characters).
typography: A serif or a refined sans for headings at modest sizes; text set for reading. No tricks.
colour: Paper-like grounds (white, off-white, a light stone) or a deep ground; ink; one muted accent at most.
imagery: Few, large, sharp photographs of one family; the pictures are the reason to keep scrolling.
richness: The writing and the pictures; every piece complete in itself.
pitfalls: Long paragraphs; every piece in the same two-column shape; captions under every picture; pull quotes nobody said.

name: The spec sheet
idea: Precision as the personality: the product or place described the way an engineer would, exactly. Dimensions, materials, tolerances, numbers and names, set beautifully. The page wins trust by being specific where everyone else is vague; find the numbers only this subject has.
composition: The first screen sets the object (or the place, or the product's output) large on a plain ground, with its name and a one-line description. Further down the page alternates between large views of the subject and well-set facts: a specification table with real rows, a numbered build or process only if order matters, a comparison of models as a clean table. A grid of details (close-up pictures with a short label naming what they show) can appear once.
typography: A precise sans; tabular figures for every number; units set properly (12 mm, 1.4 kg).
colour: Very restrained: white, grey or black ground, ink, and one accent used like a signal.
imagery: The subject photographed or generated cleanly, from the front, the side, close up; its construction shown by a close photograph of the joint or part, never a drawing. Without the client's own photographs, the subject is shown by its product statement and the close-ups show its materials, never another maker's product (the sheet's hard rule).
richness: Real, complete specifications and sharp details.
pitfalls: Invented numbers; monospace labels everywhere; a table that is really a list of marketing claims; lines and boxes around every fact.

name: The clear service
idea: People come to a service page with questions: what is it, is it for me, what does it cost, how do I start. Answer them in that order, plainly, and the page feels trustworthy. The idea is the one thing this service does that others do not, stated in the first line and proven in the rest.
composition: The first screen states what the service is and for whom, with the action (book, apply, call) and one picture of the real place or people at work. Then: who it is for, as a short list; how it works, as three or four plain steps; the prices or terms, as a table; answers to real questions, as an accordion that opens one at a time; how to reach them, with the address, hours and a map or directions. The action stays reachable on every screen.
typography: A friendly, readable sans or a warm serif for headings; text at a comfortable size.
colour: A light ground, ink, one warm or calm accent for the action.
imagery: Real pictures of the place and the people at work (the project's own, generated, or honestly generic); never stock handshakes.
richness: Complete, honest answers: the real prices, the real hours, the real steps.
pitfalls: Vague claims instead of facts; testimonials nobody gave; icons for every step; the booking hidden at the bottom.
